paragraphs: The point we have now reached for examination is the necessity, for the preservation of the Union, of a Constitution at least as energetic as the one proposed.

This inquiry will naturally divide into three branches: the objects the federal government must provide for; the amount of power needed to accomplish those objects; and the persons on whom that power ought to operate. How that power should be distributed and organized will more properly claim our attention under the next head.

The principal purposes that union must serve are these: the common defense of the members; the preservation of the public peace, against internal convulsions as well as external attacks; the regulation of commerce with other nations and among the States; and the oversight of our dealings, political and commercial, with foreign countries.

Defending the members in common requires the following authorities: to raise armies; to build and equip fleets; to prescribe the rules that govern both; to direct their operations; and to provide for their upkeep. These powers should be unlimited, BECAUSE IT IS IMPOSSIBLE TO FORESEE OR DEFINE THE EXTENT AND VARIETY OF NATIONAL EXIGENCIES, OR THE CORRESPONDENT EXTENT AND VARIETY OF THE MEANS WHICH MAY BE NECESSARY TO SATISFY THEM. There is no end to the circumstances that endanger the safety of nations, and so it would be unwise to put constitutional shackles on the power entrusted with that safety. This power should reach as far as every possible combination of such circumstances, and should be directed by the same councils that are appointed to preside over the common defense.

This is one of those truths that carry their own evidence with them to a sound and unprejudiced mind. Argument and reasoning may obscure it but cannot make it plainer. It rests on axioms as simple as they are universal: the MEANS ought to be proportioned to the END, and the persons from whose action the attainment of any END is expected ought to possess the MEANS by which it is to be attained.

Whether there ought to be a federal government entrusted with the common defense is, at the outset, an open question for discussion. But the moment it is decided in the affirmative, it follows that this government ought to be given all the powers required to carry out its trust completely. Unless it can be shown that the circumstances that may affect the public safety can be confined within certain definite limits, and unless the opposite of this position can be fairly and reasonably disputed, we must admit as a necessary consequence that there can be no limit on the authority that is to provide for the defense and protection of the community, in any matter essential to its effectiveness, that is, in any matter essential to the FORMATION, DIRECTION, or SUPPORT of the NATIONAL FORCES.

The present Confederation has proved defective, but its framers appear to have fully recognized this principle, though they did not make proper or adequate provision for exercising it. Congress has unlimited discretion to make requisitions for men and money, to govern the army and navy, and to direct their operations. Because its requisitions are made constitutionally binding on the States, which are in fact under the most solemn obligation to furnish the supplies required of them, the intention was evidently that the United States should command whatever resources they judged necessary for the "common defense and general welfare." It was assumed that a sense of their true interests and a regard for the dictates of good faith would be sufficient pledges that the members would punctually perform their duty to the federal head.

The experiment has shown, however, that this expectation was ill-founded and illusory. The observations made under the last head will, I believe, have been enough to convince the impartial and discerning that the first principles of the system must be changed entirely. If we are in earnest about giving the Union energy and durability, we must abandon the vain project of legislating for the States in their collective capacities. We must extend the laws of the federal government to the individual citizens of America. We must discard the deceptive scheme of quotas and requisitions as equally impracticable and unjust. The result of all this is that the Union ought to be given full power to levy troops, to build and equip fleets, and to raise the revenues needed to form and support an army and navy, in the customary and ordinary ways practiced in other governments.

Suppose the circumstances of our country call for a compound government instead of a simple one, a confederate government instead of a single one. The essential point left to settle will then be to distinguish, as far as possible, the OBJECTS that belong to the different provinces or departments of power, giving each the fullest authority to fulfill the objects committed to its charge. Shall the Union be made the guardian of the common safety? Are fleets, armies, and revenues necessary for this purpose? Then the government of the Union must be empowered to pass all laws and make all regulations that relate to them. The same must hold for commerce, and for every other matter to which its jurisdiction is allowed to extend. Is the administration of justice between citizens of the same State the proper department of the local governments? Then they must hold all the authorities connected with this object, and with every other that may be assigned to their particular care and direction. Not to give each, in every case, a degree of power matching its end would violate the most obvious rules of prudence and propriety, and would rashly entrust the great interests of the nation to hands that are disabled from managing them with vigor and success.

Who is more likely to make suitable provision for the public defense than the body to which the guardianship of the public safety is entrusted? As the center of information, it will best understand the extent and urgency of the dangers that threaten. As the representative of the WHOLE, it will feel itself most deeply interested in the preservation of every part. From the responsibility that goes with its assigned duty, it will be most keenly impressed with the necessity of proper exertions. And by extending its authority throughout the States, it alone can establish uniformity and concert in the plans and measures by which the common safety is to be secured. Is there not a manifest inconsistency in laying on the federal government the care of the general defense, while leaving in the State governments the EFFECTIVE powers by which it is to be provided for? Is not lack of cooperation the certain consequence of such a system? And will not weakness, disorder, an unfair distribution of the burdens and calamities of war, and an unnecessary and intolerable increase of expense be its natural and unavoidable companions? Have we not had unmistakable experience of its effects in the course of the revolution we have just accomplished?

Every view we may take of the subject, as fair inquirers after truth, will convince us that it is both unwise and dangerous to deny the federal government unconfined authority over all the objects entrusted to its management. It will indeed deserve the most vigilant and careful attention of the people to see that it is shaped in such a way that it can safely be given the requisite powers. If any plan that has been, or may be, offered for our consideration should not, on dispassionate inspection, be found to answer this description, it ought to be rejected. A government whose constitution makes it unfit to be trusted with all the powers that a free people ought to delegate to any government would be an unsafe and improper keeper of the NATIONAL INTERESTS. Wherever THESE can properly be confided, the accompanying powers may safely go with them. This is the true result of all sound reasoning on the subject. And the opponents of the plan put forward by the Convention ought to have confined themselves to showing that the internal structure of the proposed government was such as to make it unworthy of the people's confidence. They ought not to have wandered into inflammatory declamations and meaningless quibbles about the extent of the powers. The POWERS are not too extensive for the OBJECTS of federal administration, or, in other words, for the management of our NATIONAL INTERESTS; nor can any satisfactory argument be framed to show that they are chargeable with such an excess. Suppose it is true, as some of the writers on the other side have hinted, that the difficulty arises from the nature of the thing, and that the size of the country will not allow us to form a government in which such ample powers can safely be placed. That would prove that we ought to narrow our views and resort to the expedient of separate confederacies, which will move within more practicable spheres. For the absurdity must continually stare us in the face of confiding to a government the direction of the most essential national interests without daring to trust it with the authorities indispensable to their proper and effective management. Let us not try to reconcile contradictions, but firmly embrace a rational alternative.

I trust, however, that the impracticability of one general system cannot be shown. I am greatly mistaken if anything of weight has yet been advanced to that effect, and I flatter myself that the observations made in the course of these papers have placed the opposite position in as clear a light as any matter still in the womb of time and experience can be made to appear. At all events, this much must be evident: the very difficulty drawn from the extent of the country is the strongest argument in favor of an energetic government, for any other can certainly never preserve the Union of so large an empire. If we adopt the tenets of those who oppose the proposed Constitution as the standard of our political creed, we cannot fail to bear out the gloomy doctrines that predict the impracticability of a national system reaching across the entire limits of the present Confederacy.
